stories.title: At least 10 dead after two trains crashed in Spain
stories.summary: At least 10 people have died after two trains crashed south of Madrid in Spain, the regional government has said. "Two trains have collided - there are people injured," Manuel Galan, mayor of the town of Urda, told public broadcaster TVE. A spokesperson for the Spanish emergency services said the trains collided just before 9am local time (8am Irish time). "All resources are currently being deployed," the spokesperson said, including "several fire crews, three helicopters, and two mobile intensive care units". Rail infrastructure company ADIF also confirmed a collision had taken place, warning in a social media post that the high-speed rail line from "Traffic on the Madrid-Andalusia high-speed rail line has been suspended following ‌a rear-end ⁠collision between two trains," Adif said in a message posted on X.

stories.title: Patients treated abroad waiting six months for HSE refund
stories.summary: Irish patients on waiting lists here who have sought treatment in hospitals abroad, under an EU Scheme, have been left waiting six months or more in some cases to get their money back from the HSE. Patients use savings or borrow from financial institutions to pay the treatment upfront, while awaiting HSE reimbursement, and many treatments can cost over €10,000. It said the current processing can see patients wait five or six months to be repaid. The HSE's target time to complete patient applications and reimbursement is 30 working days. It said some delays can be even longer, depending on the completeness of the application and clinical complexity. The HSE said it plans to have processing times back to normal by February next year, and to have substantially reduced the backlog by the end of this year.

stories.title: Where to next after Triple Lock passes first Dáil vote?
stories.summary: The 'Triple Lock' has become one of the most contentious topics in this Government's Programme for Government, in Dáil Éireann, within the Fianna Fáil party and on the streets. But it all began when legislation was passed in 1960 to allow Irish troops to be sent abroad, after joining the United Nations five years previously. These missions would only be backed by the United Nations and for decades that meant Irish participation in peacekeeping has depended on UN backing. This rule was restated as the 'Triple Lock' at the start of the century after concerns that the Nice and Lisbon Treaties would undermine neutrality, with Government parties back then stressing its importance. Under the rule, no more than 12 troops can be deployed on an active mission overseas without a decision by the Government, the approval of the Dáil and the authorisation of the United Nations. However, because the Government usually has a majority in the Dáil, the first two conditions are largely one and the same, and UN approval became key.

stories.title: Bank of Ireland raises NII guidance again
stories.summary: Bank of Ireland said today it is on track to deliver a strong performance this year, adding that it is also on track for its 2028 financial targets. In an interim management statement for the nine months to the end of September, the bank said its total income rose by 6% while its net loans rose by 5% to €86.1 billion. Sustainable finance lending grew to €20.7 billion, up 17% so far this year, the bank noted. It added that its deposits rose by 3% to €110.3 billion, while assets under management jumped by 16% to €67 billion. The bank said its net interest income (NII) - a key banking metric - is 4% higher year to date compared to the same time last year, on the back of balance sheet growth and structural hedge benefits. Bank of Ireland said today that it was upgrading its 2026 NII guidance for the second time this year, from about €3.5 billion to more than €3.5 billion.

stories.title: Israeli elections: What happens next?
stories.summary: Israelis voted in their highest turnout in decades, with exit polls showing the camp of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and that of his rival are neck and neck. Exit polls from the three mainstream Israeli television networks gave the two blocs around 51 seats each in the 120-member Knesset, well below the 61 needed to govern, after initially giving an edge to the opposition led by ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot. Israeli Arab lists made strong gains, with exit polls showing them winning 17 or 18 seats between them. The parties will immediately begin negotiations to try to reach a 61-seat majority, but the path forward is far from clear. President Isaac Herzog will name a candidate who has the best chance to form a government, not necessarily the party with the most seats. The Arab Israeli parties, particularly Raam, have voiced openness to working with Mr Eisenkot's bloc, but the camp has kept them at arm's length, perceiving their support as a liability during the campaign.

stories.title: Ireland aiming to make fitness the 'point of difference'
stories.summary: Before the Ireland squad went their separate ways after their Nations Championship campaign closed out in New Zealand, Andy Farrell put a date in his players' diaries. An alignment camp on 31 August saw roughly 50 players brought in to Irish Rugby's high-performance centre in Dublin, a one-day gathering of those both in and around the wider Irish squad, to set their stall out for a World Cup year, while a fitness test gauges how well they had summered. In the changing room at Eden Park after Ireland's defeat to the All Blacks, Farrell told the group to turn up for session "in the right condition, ready to attack the season". "Most of the guys did that and put their best foot forward in that regard," Johnny Sexton says. The message from Farrell, according to Sexton, was clear: "It's time to ship up, get shape up, and get our act together." This time next year, Farrell and his squad will expect to be a few days out from another World Cup quarter-final.

stories.summary: Real Madrid have issued an apology ⁠after start attacker Kylian Mbappe sparked a fierce backlash over his comments referring to late Chinese leader Mao Zedong as ‌a dictator. "Our club maintains a deep ⁠respect ‌for China, its history, its culture and its citizens, as ⁠well as for the millions of ⁠Chinese fans who feel affection and admiration for Real Madrid." On Tuesday, Mbappe also apologised for comments in which he apparently referred to Mao Zedong, the founding leader of Communist China, as a dictator. stories.summary: Leinster's Tadhg Furlong has been cited for an incident with Munster's Gavin Coombes during their United Rugby Championship match on Saturday. Coombes alleged during the game that his testicles had been grabbed and despite match referee Andrew Brace asking the TMO Colin Stanley to review the incident at the time, neither could find evidence of the incident. However, since the incident was in the referee's report it could then by reviewed by the citing commissioner Peter Ferguson. "Leinster Rugby's Tadhg Furlong has been cited for an incident that occurred in the 37th minute of the United Rugby Championship Round 4 fixture at the Aviva Stadium against Munster Rugby on Saturday, October 24," a statement from the URC said. "The Citing Commissioner in charge has made a complaint about an act of foul play by the Player (Tadhg Furlong No 3) against opponent Gavin Coombes (No 8). The Player has been cited under Law 9.27 – A player must not do anything that is against the spirit of good sportsmanship including but not limited to grabbing, twisting or squeezing the genitals.

stories.title: Mayo actress Philippa Dunne on motherhood and ambition
stories.summary: "I’m shooting the Amandaland Christmas special at the moment," Philippa Dunne apologises warmly as she connects into our call from the back of a cab in London. "Like most days of filming, you think you’re going to be done by a certain time, but it always goes over. I thought I’d be home by now." There’s a buzz of energy when discussing the Amandaland festive special, which ranked as the UK’s number one comedy in 2025, pulling in over 7 million viewers. "It’s going well; we’ve one more week left, and then that’s it, it’s done," she says. "It’s only a couple of weeks of filming, but it’s good to have the gang back together. It feels fun while we’re shooting it, so I hope that transfers onto the finished product," she adds. For years, the Mayo native has been comedy television’s secret weapon, delighting audiences with her razor-sharp comic timing, warmth and gift for finding humour in the everyday. Her turn as the hopelessly eager-to-please, high-vis-vest-wearing Anne Flynn in the BBC’s Motherland made her a fan favourite, a status only cemented when she reprised the role in spin-off Amandaland. The performance proved a standout once again, earning her a BAFTA nomination. For many Irish viewers, Motherland, which was produced and written by Sharon Horgan, didn’t come onto their radar until it popped up on Netflix, after being hidden late in the BBC schedule. It was assumed that Philippa was an overnight success, but in reality it was hard-won.

stories.title: Netanyahu, Eisenkot stake rival claims to lead Israel
stories.summary: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and rival Gadi Eisenkot offered competing claims to lead Israel after yesterday's election, with Mr Netanyahu calling for a right-wing government and Mr Eisenkot saying voters had rejected the longtime Israeli leader, even as exit polls left their blocs deadlocked. While the projected results would represent ⁠a setback for Mr Netanyahu and his nationalist-religious coalition, the deadlock could work in his favour, leaving the 77-year-old in office as a caretaker prime minister during what are likely to be prolonged coalition negotiations or even until another election can beheld. With vote counts trickling in, Kan 11 and Channel 13 exit polls had the blocs tied at 51 seats each, while Channel 12 gave Mr Netanyahu's Likud-led bloc a narrow 52-49 edge. That left both sides short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, and neither Mr Netanyahu nor Mr Eisenkot claimed victory. The vote was the first election since the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023, and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. Far-right religious parties led by Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich were projected to take a combined 13 seats within Mr Netanyahu's bloc - with no major gains for either of them.

stories.title: Gardaí support work-to-rule during EU Presidency - GRA
stories.summary: Rank-and-file gardaí say they are so dissatisfied with their working conditions that they are prepared to commence a work-to-rule for the remaining events of Ireland's EU Presidency. The Garda Representative Association (GRA) has published the results of a survey of its members, which it says shows that over 90% of the gardaí who responded are prepared to take action because of their dissatisfaction. Forty five percent of their members, over 4,000 gardaí, responded to two questions about their preparedness to take part in a work-to-rule, and to do so during the EU presidency. 4,182 gardaí, or 94.2% of those who responded, said they were prepared to take industrial action, while 3,977, or 93.6%, said they would do so during the EU presidency. The GRA has accused the Garda Commissioner and Garda management of breaching the Working Time Agreement and the European Working Time Directive. GRA General Secretary Ronan Slevin said the survey shows that rank-and-file gardaí "have had enough and voiced their willingness to resist these breaches and show the Commissioner and senior Garda management that they have had enough".

stories.title: Minister says meeting with solicitors likely next week
stories.summary: The Minister for Justice has confirmed that he has "engaged" with solicitors and that a meeting is likely next week. Speaking at the launch of One In Four's annual report, Jim O’Callaghan said letters had been exchanged. A majority of solicitors working in criminal legal aid across the country have been in dispute with Mr O'Callaghan since a new €520 flat-fee payment for legal aid cases was introduced in July. Mr O’Callaghan insists that legal aid continues to be granted by the courts; solicitors continue to provide representation, and defendants continue to receive legal services throughout the State. This week, the minister said he would meet the Law Society of Ireland regarding the dispute. In a letter to President of the Law Society of Ireland Rosemarie Loftus, Mr O'Callaghan said he had instructed his officials to "organise a meeting in the coming days to hear your viewpoint and specific concerns".

stories.title: How your home loses heat
stories.summary: Analysis: Reducing heat loss begins with understanding how insulation, glazing, airtightness and ventilation all work together If your home remains uncomfortable even when its heating system is working, and some rooms cool rapidly once the heating is switched off, the explanation is often found in the building itself. Heat continually escapes to the surroundings, and the rate of that loss determines how much heating is needed to maintain comfortable conditions. According to SEAI's National Heat Study, space heating accounts for approximately 75% of residential heating demand in Ireland. Heat naturally moves from warmer places to colder ones. When a room is at 20°C and the outdoor temperature is 5°C, heat passes through the walls, roof, floor and windows. The greater the temperature difference, the faster the loss, assuming other conditions remain the same. The amount also depends on the area of each surface, its construction and the quality of the insulation. Fixed claims about the percentage of heat lost through a roof or wall can therefore be misleading. A house with uninsulated walls will behave differently from one with insulated walls and older glazing. The relative influence of walls and windows on overall energy use also varies between common Irish housing types. The appropriate improvement depends on the condition of the individual building. Windows deserve particular attention. They lose heat during cold weather but also admit sunlight, which can warm a room. Double and triple glazing reduce heat transfer by separating panes with insulating gaps, while specialist coatings help limit heat loss without excluding daylight. However, a window's performance also depends on its frame and how it meets the surrounding wall. These connections can be weak points. At the junction between a wall and floor, around a window opening or where insulation is interrupted, heat may pass through more readily than through the adjacent surface. Such areas are known as Thermal Bridges. They may also leave cold patches indoors, where moisture can condense if indoor humidity is high enough, increasing the risk of mould.

stories.title: Norway and Finland leaders hold 'frank' call with Putin
stories.summary: Finland's president and Norway's prime minister held a "frank and substantive" discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin about efforts to end the war in Ukraine, the Nordic leaders said. "The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions," Finnish President Alexander Stubb said in a joint statement with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre. Speaking to reporters in Helsinki, Mr Stubb said the idea for the call had originated during a meeting in Oslo on 20 October between Mr Støre, Mr Stubb and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky as well as US envoy Steve Witkoff. US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner also took part in the meeting remotely. After the Oslo talks, Mr Witkoff travelled to St Petersburg to meet Mr Putin. Speaking to reporters in Helsinki, where Nordic leaders are meeting, Mr Støre said the 90-minute call highlighted "big differences in views" on Ukraine.

stories.title: No Kolbe, Etzebeth or Pollard as Erasmus names Boks squad
stories.summary: Springboks head coach Rassie Erasmus has named six uncapped players in his Nations Championship squad, but will be without the services of World Cup winning trio, Cheslin Kolbe, Eben Etzebeth and Handre Pollard. The 37-man group will assemble next week ahead of a three-game window where South Africa will face Italy, France and Ireland, before the Nations Championship finals weekend in Twickenham at the end of November. If the reigning World Cup, Rugby Championship and Greatest Rivalry winners are to claim the inaugural Nations Championship crown, they will do so without marquee stars Kolbe, Etzebeth and Pollard. Their 33-year-old outside back Kolbe has not featured since the third test against New Zealand in September, while lock Etzebeth played for the Sharks against Leinster and the Stormers in the URC, but is unavailable. Out-half Pollard started in the Bulls' 34-26 win over Ulster at the weekend but is nursing an injury, while centre Andre Esterhuizen, who also misses out, was helped off the field in the Sharks' win in Edinburgh last Friday. Erasmus has included six new call-ups: Yaqeen Ahmed, Sebastian de Klerk, Luan Giliomee, Markus Muller, Riley Norton, and Emmanuel Tshituka all get the nod.

stories.title: Forde reflects on 'pride' of earning historic All-Star
stories.summary: The 2026 All Star awards will be handed out at the RDS next Friday night, with All-Ireland football champions Mayo and their hurling counterparts Limerick likely to dominate the two selections. Most players covet the Celtic Cross, but for some who haven't had the chance to play in an All-Ireland final, an All-Star award can be the highlight of a career. Wexford is one of a handful of counties that has only ever won one football All-Star; it arrived in 2004, when Matty Forde was at the peak of his powers. The Kilanerin-Ballyfad forward finished as the championship’s top scorer that season, despite only having five outings throughout the course of the campaign. His 2-10 haul against Offaly in a qualifier at Wexford Park was a particular highlight; he also notched the same tally in a league match against Sligo, before netting four goals in a single match against Galway that same spring. His displays were also recognised when he was crowned as the 2004 GPA Footballer of the Year. "Is there a sense of pride in it now? Absolutely," Forde said.

stories.title: Ballon d'Or chaos as winners 'leaked' before ceremony
stories.summary: The Ballon d'Or website has published three separate articles naming Harry Kane, Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe as winner of the 2026 men’s award. Hours before the ceremony for the 70th edition of the individual accolade at Palladium Theatre in London, chaos descended when a link emerged announcing England captain Kane had received the honour. "A record-breaking welter of league and cup goals in 2025/26 has propelled Harry Kane to Ballon d’Or success," read the story on the official website of the prestigious France Football prize. However, further links were subsequently found to articles hailing Real Madrid forward Mbappe and Barcelona winger Yamal as victors. !Portraits of some Ballon d'Or nominees prepared by Ballondor.com were inadvertently published online," the organisers said in a statement. "These articles had been prepared in advance for all nominees in the event of a win. They do not, in any way, reveal the podium, which remains unknown to everyone at this time."

stories.title: Leatherbarrow in line for first Scotland cap
stories.summary: Newcastle back-rower Ollie Leatherbarrow has been called up by Scotland for the first time for next month's Nations Championship fixtures. The English-born 24-year-old, who qualifies through his grandmother from Perth, is the most notable inclusion in a largely familiar 37-man pool named by Gregor Townsend for matches at Murrayfield against New Zealand, Australia and Japan. Glasgow hooker Seb Stephen, who made his debut in the summer, has kept his place alongside other recent additions to the forward pack, Liam McConnell and Gregor Hiddleston. Senior trio Jamie Ritchie, Darcy Graham and Duhan van der Merwe have all been included after returning recently from injuries. stories.title: They did not go quietly - inside Ireland's last witch trial
stories.summary: It’s May 2026 and we are driving on a sunny weekday afternoon to the Islandmagee Peninsula, twenty miles north of Belfast. As the waters of Larne Lough, the body of water which separates Islandmagee from the mainland, comes into view the question arises, what do we believe really happened here on this remote spit of land back in 1711? The history books tell us that a young Presbyterian woman named Mary Dunbar was showing all the signs of demonic possession. Over a period of days, she named eight local women as witches, claiming they were responsible for her torment. The people of Islandmagee, at that time mostly Presbyterians of Scottish descent, believed Mary's accusations and the eight women were arrested, put on trial and found guilty. They are on record as fiercely protesting their innocence in court. Today the peninsula is a tourist attraction for visitors to the Gobbins, a cliff walkway suspended over the Irish Sea. Yet, there are traces of its past written into the landscape; stone built cottages clinging to hillsides, churches dating back to the 1500s, and a landmark steeped in folklore: the Witches’ Rocking Stone, a boulder overlooking Brown’s Bay.

stories.title: Star Trek's William Shatner pays tribute to Walter Koenig
stories.summary: William Shatner has remembered his Star Trek co-star Walter Koenig and said he was "deeply saddened" to learn of his death aged 90. Koenig, who starred in the original 1960s sci-fi series as Russian crewman Ensign Pavel Chekov, died at his home in North Hollywood on Sunday night, according to his talent agency, Galactic Productions. His death was announced in a Facebook post that remembered Koenig's legacy and career as being full of "talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances", which left a "lasting mark on generations of fans around the world". Shatner, 95, who played Captain James T Kirk in the franchise, wrote in a post on Instagram: "I am deeply saddened to learn of Walter Koenig's passing. "Although we did not know each other well away from the set, we shared the later seasons of the original Star Trek series and the six films that followed. "What I observed, and what so many fans have expressed over the years, was a man who genuinely loved the Star Trek community.

stories.title: Room rotting: Learning to holiday as an overachieving millennial
stories.summary: There are two things everyone who knows me can agree on: One, I'm always late. Two, I’m a gold-star millennial. Like most women in their early thirties, my sexual awakening came courtesy of Jeremy Sumpter in the 2003 live-action remake of Peter Pan. I start my day with a healthy dose of existential dread and an oat cappuccino. I love Taylor Swift. My approach to travel has been equally stereotypical. As a semi-reformed Instagram tourist, I’ve jetted around the world collecting world wonders like Clubcard points, caring more about taking a picture of Santorini's (underwhelming) blue-domed roofs or pretending to be Lizzie McGuire at the Colosseum than travelling mindfully. Queuing for over two hours for a picture at Bali’s Gate of Heaven, only to discover the lake I’d seen on social media was all smoke and literal mirrors, was a particular low point. That’s not to say I’m a shallow traveller. If anything, I’m guilty of cramming in every museum, landmark, or semi-significant pothole, to then leave a destination completely exhausted. Gen Z, however, seem to be doing things a little differently, swapping bucket lists and jam-packed itineraries for 'room rotting’ - a travel trend highlighted in a recent 2026 Airbnb report. According to the research, two-thirds of Gen Z travellers are now going on holiday with the intention of doing absolutely nothing, while 8 in 10 spend at least half their trip at their accommodation. The home becomes the whole point of the trip.

stories.title: Court to rule on NI secretary banning Garvaghy Road march
stories.summary: A Belfast court will rule today whether the Northern Ireland Secretary of State was right to ban an Orange Order parade from the predominately nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown. Chris Bryant made the decision earlier this month following a weeklong nationalist counter protest to prevent the Drumcree parade. The Portadown District of the Orange Order challenged that decision in the courts. It had been given permission by the Parades Commission for an early morning, silent procession by 35 of its members along the Garvaghy Road. The High Court in Belfast is scheduled to hand down its judgment this morning. The court was told that by 9 October the police believed all available, lawful and proportionate ways to facilitate the parade had been exhausted.

stories.title: Location-specific weather warning system delayed
stories.summary: A plan for a new weather-warning system that focuses on more specific locations rather than counties will not be in place this year, but some changes that "support more localised weather warnings" as part of the plan have been implemented. The new system, which had been planned for rollout by the end of this year, is still in the consulting phase, according to Met Éireann. The changes will see polygons or shapes on maps that will be used to focus on specific areas rather than entire counties being issued with warnings. The Department of Housing, Local Government, and Heritage previously said the system will be "more relevant to communities", and that it will "will provide clearer direction to those at risk and support more targeted emergency preparedness" when implemented. A spokesperson for Met Éireann said the consultation phase will see the plan put through focus groups, as well as more research and consultation with Government departments. Work is continuing to restore power to the remaining homes, farms and businesses that lost supply during Storm Boelo.

stories.title: No measure can ease pain of scoliosis failures - minister
stories.summary: The Minister for Health has acknowledged that no measures the Government may introduce will alleviate the pain endured by those affected by failures in spina bifida and scoliosis services. She told the Dáil that stakeholders will be consulted by her officials, who will work with the Attorney General to draft terms of reference for a commission of inquiry. The minister was speaking during Statements on Children's Health Ireland (CHI), which was also attended in the visitors' gallery by some of those who have been advocating for action on the matter. Ms Carroll MacNeill said that she received the final scoping report on 9 September, and expressed her gratitude to Remy Farrell SC for his efforts to "capture the pain" and "very real frustration" of those affected. She noted that a commission of investigation, as recommended by Mr Farrell, allows for greater flexibility than a tribunal, including private hearings. She noted that witnesses can request whether to have their testimony heard in public or private.

stories.title: Stellantis posts modest Q3 operating income, burns €4bn
stories.summary: Stellantis has today posted a slight increase in operating income in the third quarter as the automaker presses ahead with a slow turnaround process, which still generated a €4 billion industrial cash outflow in the period. Following two years of sliding sales and profitability, CEO Antonio Filosa in May promised dozens of new models, cost cuts and deeper cooperation with Chinese partners as part of a new business plan up until 2030. However, investors still need to be convinced that the Franco-Italian automaker, which in February announced EV-related impairments for over €22 billion, is on the path to sustained recovery. Earlier this month its shares sank to their lowest level since the group's formation in early 2021 through the Fiat Chrysler-Peugeot merger. The Fiat-to-Jeep maker said its adjusted earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) amounted to €256m in the three months from July to September, from €90m a year earlier. That was broadly in line with a consensus of €191m from a Reuters poll of analysts, who were bracing for a weak quarter before an expected stronger performance in the final part of the year.

stories.title: Africa Ebola outbreak passes 10,000 confirmed cases
stories.summary: Africa's latest outbreak of Ebola has passed 10,000 confirmed cases, the vast majority of them in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the Congolese health authorities said, resulting in almost 5,000 fatalities. According to the DRC's figures, 10,060 people have been infected and 4,887 have died since the virus was first detected in May in the vast central African country's deadliest outbreak in its history. Cases have likewise been detected in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda, with the World Health Organization (WHO) warning that Africa faces a "complex" task to contain an outbreak spanning the east, west and centre of the continent. While some 2,684 have recovered from the virus in the DRC, the epidemic's fatality rate appears to be close to 50%, according to the Congolese National Institute of Public Health. Among the many challenges facing the response is the lack of any approved vaccines or treatments for the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the epidemic. After spreading under the radar for weeks, the virus was first detected in the northeastern Congolese province of Ituri, kicking off the DRC's 17th outbreak of the disease.

stories.title: Fleetwood dump PL champions Arsenal out of Carabao Cup
stories.summary: League Two Fleetwood shocked Premier League champions Arsenal in a penalty shoot-out to advance to the Carabao Cup quarter-finals after a 1-1 draw. Bruno Guimaraes saw his spot-kick saved by Jay Lynch before Fleetwood's teenage defender Conor Haughey lashed home an emphatic penalty to spark a pitch invasion at Highbury Stadium as Fleetwood triumphed 5-3 in one of the greatest upsets in the competition’s history. There's a strong Irish connection to Fleetwood with manager Matt Lawlor formerly taking charge of Waterford FC in 2025. Limerick's Ronan Coughlan, who played for a multitude of League of Ireland clubs, scored in the shoot-out and Haughey plays for the Northern Ireland Under-21s. "Amazing for the club, the town. Honestly it means everything to everyone," Lynch told Sky. "We took heart from Grimsby beating Man Utd last year. We kind of compared it. The whole team throughout the game was magnificent. To beat the English champions - credit to these lads." Fleetwood, 18th in League Two, dared to dream after Fulham loanee Aaron Loupalo-Bi put them in front after 21 minutes against a much-changed Arsenal side struggling to find any fluidity on the Fylde coast.
